description: Hi! I'm Aslıhan, a  Bioengineering student experienced in biosensor design and Python data modeling. Team LEFT CORNER is tackling the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts" challenge! We aim to build a non-invasive biometric tracking software concept for space missions.
summary:
SignalCheck is a personalized health assistant for astronauts on deep-space missions. It interprets vital signs, symptoms and cabin conditions against each astronaut’s own health history and reference ranges. In our Mars transit simulation, the same heart rate of 105 bpm falls within one astronaut’s personal range and above another’s. The assistant asks follow-up questions, shows which measurements are missing and flags cases that need onboard medical review.

The crew can open and review a case offline. When communication is available, an Earth-based doctor can review the case and its supporting measurements, write a consultation note and send it back to the same case after a simulated delay. NASA spaceflight research and Earth-based wearable sensor studies informed the design. The demonstration uses synthetic astronaut records, measurements and consultations.
details:
LEFT CORNER built SignalCheck for a practical problem on deep-space missions. When an astronaut feels unwell and a doctor on Earth cannot respond immediately, the crew needs to understand what has changed for that astronaut, what evidence is missing and when to ask for medical review.

Personalized health assistant. SignalCheck gives each astronaut an individual health profile and reference ranges. The same heart rate of 105 bpm falls within Maya’s personal reference range and above Elias’s. The assistant combines that comparison with reported symptoms, measurement quality and cabin context. It asks structured follow-up questions and identifies measurements that need verification. In one demonstration, it flags missing oxygen saturation and blood pressure and explains why a carbon dioxide reading from another compartment leaves the astronaut’s exposure uncertain.

Onboard review and Earth consultation. The crew can save and review a case locally during a communications outage. An independent safety check can interrupt the routine questions and open an emergency case for the onboard Crew Medical Officer. The crew can then queue the case for Earth. In the Earth Medical Doctor view, a reviewer can open a received case, inspect its supporting measurements and assessment, and write a consultation note. The note returns to the original case after the simulated communication delay. When the link is unavailable, the transfer pauses and the onboard case remains accessible.

Research and development. NASA Human Research Program and Exploration Medical Capability resources informed the mission context and the onboard review workflow. Earth-based wearable sensor research informed how we handle measurement quality and missing evidence. We also identified open terrestrial PPG, motion and reference ECG data as a candidate for future sensor-quality testing. We built a self-contained browser prototype with React and TypeScript. Its assessments use predefined rules, and the demonstration uses synthetic profiles, measurements and consultations. AI tools assisted research synthesis, development and presentation design.
